entry.title: Self-interactions as a window onto ultralight dark matter couplings

link.title: Self-interactions as a window onto ultralight dark matter couplings

entry.content:
Today I gave the APEC seminar at Kavli IPMU on our recent paper with S. Li, Self-Interaction Bounds on Ultralight Dark Matter Couplings to Matter. Here is the idea in a nutshell.

Ultralight dark matter (ULDM) is a framework where particle physics, astrophysics and cosmology meet. Its couplings to Standard Model particles and its self-interactions are usually treated as two separate things, each with its own searches and bounds.

But they are not independent. Any coupling of ULDM to ordinary matter radiatively induces a self-interaction of the dark matter field. Since cosmological and astrophysical observations constrain ULDM self-interactions very strongly, and robustly, those limits can be turned into indirect constraints on how ULDM talks to the Standard Model.

As a proof of principle, this connection gives:

  • strong limits on linear couplings to neutrinos, in the parameter space relevant for neutrino-oscillation searches for ULDM;
  • limits on quadratic couplings to electrons and light quarks that can compete with, or even exceed, those from equivalence-principle tests.

In the talk I also discussed the assumptions behind the argument, possible objections such as radiative stability and naturalness, and how far the bounds can be evaded. The broader lesson is that the extraordinary sensitivity of cosmology to ULDM self-interactions may be a powerful and largely unexplored window onto its couplings to the Standard Model.

More talks are listed on the talks page.

entry.title: 248 keV: a familiar number in the LZ data

link.title: 248 keV: a familiar number in the LZ data

entry.content:
Last week, while reading papers about the new LZ result, I kept seeing the same number: 248 keV.

At some point on Thursday, I thought: this number looks very familiar.

I remembered a paper I had read some time ago pointing out that bound neutrons in heavy nuclei typically carry momenta of order 250 MeV. If such a neutron suddenly disappears, that momentum is inherited by the residual xenon nucleus. A quick back-of-the-envelope estimate gives a nuclear recoil of about 250 keV, remarkably close to the 248 keV event reported by LZ.

On Saturday night I emailed Alessandro Strumia with the idea and my calculations. We started exchanging calculations and drafts, and by Monday evening we had most of a paper. 🙂

I’m very happy to share the result:

Neutron disappearance and the LZ nuclear recoil event
M. Aghaie and A. Strumia, arXiv:2609.09037

We explore whether the 248 keV LZ nuclear recoil event could originate from the disappearance of a bound neutron, either through spontaneous neutron decay or through a dark-matter-induced reaction.

A particularly interesting possibility occurs for near-threshold, DM-induced neutron disappearance: the process can be kinematically open in xenon while remaining closed in oxygen, and the nuclear recoil spectrum turns from a broad distribution into characteristic lines.

Whether or not this event ultimately has anything to do with neutron disappearance, this was a fun reminder of why unexpected experimental events are worth staring at carefully, and why sometimes recognizing a familiar number is enough to start a new calculation.

Read the paper on arXiv. I hope you enjoy reading it!
